Patient Vignette: Priya

Priya is a 61-year-old married South Asian woman who has worked as an agricultural laborer in the Central Valley for over thirty years. She presents to therapy at the urging of her adult daughter, who has noticed her mother "isn't herself anymore." Priya sits with her hands folded tightly in her lap, her eyes fixed on a spot on the floor. She speaks in a soft, measured voice, often pausing to gather herself.

The event that changed everything happened fourteen months ago, in the late summer. Priya was working alone in a remote corner of a tomato field, picking the last of the season's crop before dusk. The field was vast and quiet, the only sounds the rustle of leaves and the distant hum of a tractor. A man she recognized as a seasonal supervisor approached her, asking for help with a broken irrigation line. She trusted him—she had seen him around the fields for years, had even shared a cup of chai with him during a break once. When she followed him behind a row of tall corn, he turned on her.

She remembers the weight of his body, the smell of sweat and diesel, the feel of gravel digging into her back. She remembers praying to the gods she has worshipped her whole life, asking them to make it stop. She remembers the silence afterward, how he simply stood up, zipped his pants, and walked away without a word. She lay there for what felt like hours, staring at the fading sky, unable to move. When she finally got up, she did not tell anyone. She went home, showered, and cooked dinner for her husband, just as she had done for thirty-eight years.

In the weeks that followed, Priya began to change. She stopped going to the temple, a place she had visited every Tuesday for as long as she could remember. The smell of incense, once comforting, now made her nauseous. She could not bear to have her husband touch her, even a hand on her shoulder. She began sleeping in the living room, claiming she had back pain. She started flinching at the sound of a tractor backfiring, or when a man’s voice called out to her from across the field. She began working shorter shifts, claiming fatigue, but the truth was she could not bear to be in the field after 4 PM, when the light began to slant and the shadows grew long.

Her mind replays the event in fragments, like a film reel stuck on a single, horrifying frame. She will be washing dishes and suddenly feel his breath on her neck. She will be walking to the market and see a man in a blue shirt—the same color he wore—and her heart will pound so hard she has to lean against a wall. She avoids the road that leads to that field, taking a longer, dustier path instead. She has not told her husband. She cannot. In their community, she believes, such a thing would bring shame upon her family, upon her daughters. She would be seen as spoiled, as complicit.

Now, in session, Priya’s hands tremble as she describes a recurring nightmare: she is drowning in a sea of red tomatoes, their skins bursting against her skin, while a faceless figure watches from the edge. She wakes up gasping, drenched in sweat, and does not sleep again. She has lost twelve pounds. Her daughter found her crying in the bathroom one morning, clutching a bar of soap so hard her knuckles were white. Priya cannot say the word "rape." She calls it "the bad thing," and even then, she looks away.

She still goes to the fields, because there is no choice. Her family needs the money. But she works in terror, her eyes constantly scanning the horizon, her body coiled like a spring. She carries a small knife in her pocket now, a secret she has never told anyone. She is not sure if she would use it on him, or on herself.
